---
title: "Standard Normal (μ = 0, σ = 1)"
subtitle: "The control case: a population that is already normal"
---

```{r}
#| label: simulate
#| code-summary: "Show the simulation code"
source("../R/clt_functions.R")

rgen  <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
mu    <- 0
sigma <- 1

coarse <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100)
exper  <- run_with_refinement(rgen, coarse, mu, sigma)

res    <- exper$results
n_main <- smallest_normal_n(res)
n_std  <- n_by_standard(res)
at     <- function(k) res[res$n == k, ]

save_results(res, "normal")
save_summary(res, "Normal(0,1)", n_main, prediction = "1",
             key_note = "Control case: normal at every n")
```

::: {.answer-box}
<span class="big">n = `r n_main`</span> under my main standard
(strict standard: `r n_std[["strict"]]` · lenient standard: `r n_std[["lenient"]]` · my prediction: 1)
:::

## 1. What population am I sampling from?

The standard normal distribution: the bell curve itself. It is symmetric, has no skewness, and its tails
are exactly as heavy as the normal benchmark. It is the **control case** of the study: if the simulation
and the diagnostics work correctly, the sample means should pass every check at every sample size.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean μ | 0 |
| Standard deviation σ | 1 |
| Skewness | 0 |
| Excess kurtosis | 0 |
| Theoretical SE of the mean | 1/√n |

```{r}
#| label: fig-population
#| fig-cap: "The population: 100,000 draws from N(0, 1) with the true density."
#| fig-height: 4
set.seed(student_id)
style_par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
x <- rnorm(100000)
hist(x, breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, col = adjustcolor(pal$bars, 0.75),
     border = "white", main = "", xlab = "Value", ylab = "Density")
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = pal$curve, lwd = 2.2)
```

## 2. What did I expect before running the simulation?

> **n = 1.** The population is already normal, and in my pilot run every check passed at n = 1.
> A mean of independent normal values is itself exactly normal, so there is nothing to wait for.

## 3. Which sample sizes did I investigate?

n = `r paste(coarse, collapse = ", ")`, with **B = 100,000** sample means per n and seed `r student_id`.
Since n = 1 already passes, no refinement stage was needed.

## 4. Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-convergence
#| fig-cap: "The four checks stay inside the pass zone at every n."
#| fig-height: 6.5
plot_convergence(res, chosen_n = n_main, theory_skew = 0, theory_kurt = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist
#| fig-cap: "Sampling distribution of the mean (bars) and the CLT normal curve (red)."
#| fig-height: 3.4
plot_hist_grid(exper, c(1, 5, 30), mu, sigma)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq
#| fig-cap: "Normal Q-Q plots: straight lines at every n."
#| fig-height: 3.4
plot_qq_grid(exper, c(1, 5, 30))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-se
#| fig-cap: "Simulated SE (dots) against σ/√n (line)."
#| fig-height: 4.2
plot_se_check(res)
```

The simulated mean stayed within `r f4(max(abs(res$sim_mean - mu)))` of 0, and the simulated SE stayed
within `r pct(max(abs(res$se_ratio - 1)))` of 1/√n at every sample size.

## 5. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r n_main`}$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-standards
#| echo: false
standards_table(res)
```

## 6. Why did I choose that value?

- At n = 1 the skewness is `r f3(at(1)$skewness)`, the excess kurtosis `r f3(at(1)$ex_kurtosis)`,
  the Q-Q correlation `r f4(at(1)$qq_cor)`, and the tails are `r pct(at(1)$lower_tail, 2)` /
  `r pct(at(1)$upper_tail, 2)`, all essentially perfect. The same holds at every larger n.
- Even the Shapiro-Wilk test, which I do not use for decisions because it is very sensitive,
  rejected normality at the 5% level for only `r sum(res$shapiro_p < 0.05)` of the
  `r nrow(res)` sample sizes. That is about what chance alone would produce for truly normal data.
- This confirms the tools: on data that really are normal, my simulation and my four checks
  do not create false alarms. That makes the failures in the other populations meaningful.

## 7. What surprised me?

> This one was not a surprise. The sample means were normal already at n = 1 under all three standards,
> which makes sense because averaging normal values always gives a normal result. It was also a useful
> check that my simulation code was not distorting anything.
